chapter.title: The turn: three battles that stopped the spread

cards.body: In eight months, from June 1942 to February 1943, the Axis stopped winning, and not one of the battles that did it ended the war. On our street, this is when the neighbours stop the flames from reaching the next house. **A turning point is a firebreak, not the fire going out**: each battle took away one thing the Axis needed to keep spreading.
cards.simpler: In eight months, from June 1942 to February 1943, the Axis stopped winning. Yet none of the battles that did it ended the war. Think of neighbours on a street stopping flames before they reach the next house. **A turning point is a firebreak, not the fire going out**: a gap the flames can't cross. Each battle took away one thing the Axis needed to keep spreading.

cards.prompt: It's Saturday night. A kitchen fire on Elm Row has already taken two houses. Five neighbours with garden hoses are on the pavement. What's the first real sign that they're winning?

options.text: The flames stop jumping to the third house.
The fire reaches the end of the street.

whyNot.b: That's putting it out, not the turn: the first house can smoke for hours after the spread has stopped.
whyNot.c: That's the fire winning, not the turn: reaching the end of the street means nothing stopped it.

cards.reteach: A fire is beaten in two stages. First you stop it spreading. Much later, the last ember goes out. The war worked the same way, and 1942 to 1943 was stage one.

cards.title: Two firebreaks: sea and desert
cards.body:
The first break came at sea. At Midway, a tiny American island in the middle of the Pacific, Japan lost four aircraft carriers in June 1942. Those were the floating airfields its whole advance depended on. After that, Japan was **guarding what it had taken, not taking more**.

The second came in the desert. At El Alamein in Egypt, in October and November 1942, Bernard Montgomery's British Eighth Army pushed back Erwin Rommel's German and Italian army.

Rommel had been heading for the Suez Canal, Britain's shortcut to India and to Middle East oil. He never got there.
cards.simpler:
The first break came at sea. At Midway, a tiny American island in the Pacific, Japan lost four aircraft carriers in June 1942. Its whole advance relied on these floating airfields. After that, Japan was **guarding what it had taken, not taking more**.

The second break came in Egypt's desert, at El Alamein, in late 1942. Montgomery's British army pushed back Rommel's German and Italian army, which never reached the Suez Canal, Britain's shortcut to India and Middle East oil.

cards.title: The island that ran out of water
cards.body: In May 1942, American codebreakers in Hawaii could read parts of Japan's navy messages, and those messages kept naming a target called *AF*. The codebreakers suspected AF was Midway, so Midway was told to send a fake message saying its water plant had broken. Soon after, a Japanese message reported that **AF was short of water**. So when Japan's carriers arrived in June, three American carriers were already waiting for them. One pretend broken water plant, four sunk carriers.
cards.simpler: In May 1942, American codebreakers in Hawaii, people who crack secret codes, could read parts of Japan's navy messages. Those messages kept naming a target called *AF*. Suspecting it was Midway, they had Midway send a fake message saying its water plant had broken. Soon a Japanese message reported that **AF was short of water**. So when Japan's carriers arrived in June, three American carriers were waiting. One pretend broken water plant, four sunk carriers.

cards.prompt: Your friend Priya is making a pub quiz and needs one line on why El Alamein mattered. Which line belongs on the card?

options.text: It stopped Rommel from reaching the Suez Canal.
It sank four Japanese aircraft carriers.
It ended all the fighting in North Africa for good.

whyNot.b: That's Midway, not El Alamein: the carriers went down in the Pacific, not the Egyptian desert.
whyNot.c: That's putting the fire out, not the firebreak: El Alamein stopped an advance. It didn't finish every fight.

cards.reteach: For each battle, ask what it stopped. Midway stopped Japan from taking more of the Pacific. El Alamein stopped Rommel's march east to the canal.

cards.title: The biggest break, and the hidden one
cards.body:
In summer 1942, Germany drove south inside the Soviet Union towards the oil fields of the Caucasus, and turned aside to take Stalingrad, a city on the Volga river. In November, Soviet armies closed around the city like a pair of tongs.

Hitler made the trapped commander, Friedrich Paulus, a field marshal. It was a hint, because no German field marshal had ever surrendered. Paulus surrendered the next day, and by 2 February 1943 it was over. About 91,000 Germans were taken prisoner. Only around 5,000 ever came home.

Under it all ran the water main: **the supply ships crossing the Atlantic**. In May 1943, German submarines lost so many boats that they were pulled out of the North Atlantic.
cards.simpler:
In 1942, Germany drove into the Soviet Union for oil and turned to take Stalingrad, on the Volga. In November, Soviet armies closed around it like tongs. Hitler made the trapped commander, Paulus, a field marshal, since none had ever surrendered. Paulus surrendered next day. It ended on 2 February 1943. About 91,000 Germans were captured; around 5,000 came home.

Underneath ran **the Atlantic supply ships**. By May 1943, German submarines had lost so many boats they left the North Atlantic.

cards.body: Tom reads about Stalingrad, closes the book, and asks why Germany didn't give up in February 1943. You'd think a turning point means the end is close. Here it meant two more years of fighting. To catch this mistake, ask of any battle **what did this stop?**, not what did it finish?
cards.simpler: Tom reads about Stalingrad, shuts the book, and asks why Germany didn't give up in February 1943. It's easy to think a turning point means the end is near. Here it meant two more years of fighting. To avoid this mistake, ask of any battle **what did this stop?**, not what did it finish?

cards.prompt: It's February 1943 and Stalingrad has just fallen. A man reading the newspaper in a London café asks what has actually changed. Which answer is best?

options.text: The war is basically over. Germany will surrender by the summer.
Germany has lost its push for the Caucasus oil, and a whole army with it.
Japan has lost its aircraft carriers, so Germany is beaten.

whyNot.a: That's the fire going out, not the firebreak: Germany fought on until May 1945.
whyNot.c: That's Midway, not Stalingrad: Midway stopped Japan in the Pacific, not Germany in the Soviet Union.

cards.reteach: Each of the three battles took one specific thing off the table. Stalingrad took the Caucasus oil out of Germany's reach and cost it about 91,000 prisoners. Stopped, not finished.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
Between June 1942 and February 1943, three battles **stopped the Axis spreading**: Midway ended Japan's run in the Pacific, El Alamein kept Rommel from the Suez Canal, and Stalingrad cost Germany its push for oil and a whole army. Underneath, the supply ships kept crossing the Atlantic, and by May 1943 the German submarines had lost that fight too.

Tomorrow: how the Allies landed in Normandy while Germany watched somewhere else.
cards.simpler:
Between June 1942 and February 1943, three battles **stopped the Axis spreading**. Midway ended Japan's run in the Pacific. El Alamein kept Rommel from the Suez Canal. Stalingrad cost Germany its push for oil and a whole army. Underneath, supply ships kept crossing the Atlantic, and by May 1943 the German submarines had lost that fight too.

Tomorrow: how the Allies landed in Normandy while Germany watched somewhere else.

cards.body: Open the maps app on your phone. Find El Alamein, the Suez Canal, and Volgograd, which is Stalingrad's name today. Notice how close Rommel got to the canal, and how far Stalingrad is from Berlin.
cards.simpler: Open the maps app on your phone. Search for El Alamein, the Suez Canal, and Volgograd, which is what Stalingrad is called today. First, look at **how close Rommel got to the canal**. Then look at how far Stalingrad is from Berlin, Germany's capital.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now name the three battles of 1942 and 1943 and say exactly what each one stopped the Axis from doing.
